new_statements.relation_note: Catalog (StressTyp2) records final stress (final stress). Henderson's 'pretonic' first syllable and 'weak stress on the first syllable' of disyllables place the tonic on the final syllable, consistent with the catalog; it adds only the phonetic correlate (first-syllable vowel reduced to y [ɨ]) and gives no explicit rule for longer words or loans.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No stress rule is stated as such; the paper is about morphology. Incidental remarks consistently treat the first syllable of phonetically disyllabic words (Cy- prefix/infix words, lexicalized compounds) as pretonic / weakly stressed with the reduced vowel y [ɨ], i.e. the tonic (stressed) syllable is the final, stem syllable; proclitic particles are unstressed relative to the following noun. This implies word-final (stem-final) prominence in modern Standard Khasi (Cherrapunji).
new_statements.exceptions: None as a stress rule. Notes that some compounds are still sometimes pronounced/felt as two full words (khunlung, khunnah alongside khyllung, khynnah), i.e. reduction of the first element is a matter of lexicalization; speakers distinguish jynkieng 'bridge' (reduced) from jingkieng 'shoulder strap' (unreduced prefix).
new_statements.identity_note: Henderson describes 'modern Standard Khasi', defined (sec. 0.1, p.477) as the educated speech and written language of Cherrapunji (Sohra); informants Namita Shadap Sen, Renée Jyrwa, Ivan Simon. Passing mentions of Pnar, Mnar, Lamin and 'W. Khasi' dialect forms are lexical comparisons only.

audit.reasoning: Quote check passes in both held carriers ( passage 1177; Schiering & van der Hulst 2010 pp.592 and 594, verbatim, pages verified from footers). The classification 'final, fixed-dominant, non-strict, domain word and phrase together' matches every statement seen: Rabel via StressTyp2 (final stress in isolation, deleted in context except on the last word), Khyriem 2001 via the survey (final accent in simple/complex/compound words), and held Nagaraja 1990 p.26 (stress contextual/emphatic — supports the word and phrase together caution rather than a different position); held Nagaraja 1977 phonology chapter has no stress section. Weaknesses: the chain is second-hand (database + survey quoting a 1961 grammar and an unpublished 2001 MA), Rabel p.30 is not yet obtained, and the 2014 Brill sketch by Nagaraja is unread; the survey itself flags the status of Khasi 'stress' as 'highly debatable'.
